en: The people gathered to speak,
Placed a golden crown upon him,
Seated him on a golden throne,
The people loved him and made him their lord.
Roused by honor, that child
Began to wreak havoc.
When he reached twelve this year,
One arm of Toobalban
He tore clean out.
No one brought him trouble;
Among the peoples of eight khans
None remained who could answer back.
He kept a court and became khan,
Became an established judge.
In renowned Bukhara,
At twelve years old he became khan.
Whoever answered him defiantly,
He seized and twisted their neck.
The many people of populous Bukhara
He ruled at twelve.
Is Bukhara the land where you dwell,
Who made so many fervent wishes?
My dear Kanykei,
Is this your little brother?
When fortune has left our heads,
My young kinsman by marriage, is this a time to rise to the heights?
You became lord of your people.
Though I have not seen or known you,
My dear young kinsman by marriage, are you well?
Young kinsman, ride over and visit our home.
'How are you faring?' ask,
And visit this dark-fated soul!
Do not let the whip-bearer strike me,
Do not let the winged one beat me.
This lonely head of golden worth,
Do not let the grasping bird devour it.
They are such a gossiping people:
Here in Bukhara,
Do not let them call me a wandering woman.
Let me see your face.
'Kinswoman by marriage, how do you fare?'
Keep asking after me.
Ride over and call at our home,
Keep asking how I fare.
Temir Khan, khan of Bukhara,
Ismail and Semetey,
Upon you three in Bukhara
We rely for support.
Poor widows like us
Find peace when you ride over to visit.
'May all three stay safe and well,'
We keep asking God!'
Speaking without letting her secret show,
Voicing a secret no one could know,
Grasping him firmly about the neck,
Burning him with her words,
Her mouth to his throat
She touched ever so lightly.
Drawing in his scent with a deep sniff,
The old mistress left in misery
Had no way to speak openly.
She breathed his scent deeply.
Helpless, without recourse,
'The only one left by the magnanimous hero,' she thought.
Your noble mother Chiyrdy
Could not burst out wailing.
Letting go of the child,
Your mother then sank into troubled thoughts.
The spring flowing from the ridge,
She looked him in the face,
The orphan left by the champion.
Her thoughts more deeply troubled,
Chiyrdy beheld as a living memento
That child left by the champion.
When she beheld his blessing,
Her rib bones came apart.
The old woman at death's door
Felt her heart sorely torn.
Every bone ached piercingly.
There was no way to weep openly.
'The orphan left by the ocean,' she thought,
And the old woman turned away,
Wailing and sobbing.
Her poor heart torn apart,
At the place where she saw the child,
Bloody tears mixed with blood
Poured upon her breast.
As the old woman wailed,
Her voice reached God.
Your venerable grandmother,
The old mistress staggered
And fell, turning away.
Unable to keep looking at her ocean,
The old mistress lost consciousness.
As though she would face the Last Judgment,
A hard day fell upon her,
As though she would die in an instant.
Her voice reached God.
The poor old mistress
Fell upon the bed.
Hunching like a quail,
The old mistress curled up.
Bending double,
The old mistress sank down.
Letting the tears stream,
The old mistress lay shedding them.
At the sight of her only son,
The old mistress was wasting away.
Wailing, bent over,
The venerable old mistress—
Let us leave her here.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Let us begin to tell of the noble one.
Your honored sister-in-law Kanykei,
She is the very eye of the Night of Power.
Torment six months away,
She could see this very moment;
She was a true saint.
If this sister-in-law grew angry,
She made her towering head a banner,
Made a warrior of her woman's self.
A cultivator of wisdom, bringing good fortune,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Strong beyond others, bringing good fortune,
Placed in the lead, was like a myriad troops.
If you relied upon your sister-in-law,
But for being a woman,
With her watching over you, she was like a myriad troops.
Finding words in a sudden crisis,
The aged Chiyrdy,
Without leaving her to lament in burning grief,
To the child left by Manas,
Of the wailing old woman
She concealed that she was his grandmother.
Sharpening her eloquent tongue,
Was she not your fair-minded sister-in-law,
Speaking like a songbird before the khan?
Speaking on, turning the talk aside,
Her words were sugar, her tongue was honey.
My wise elder sister Kanykei
Began to speak with fitting words,
Speaking softly, laying her words firmly,
Began with words sweeter than sugar:
'My dear little brother,
My mother is ninety-five.
When I see her, my heart is at peace.
This revered mother whom you see,
If this mother of mine were gone,
Your lamenting elder sister—
How could she have any life to live?
My brow is filled with heavy misfortune.
Your elder sister's sorrow
Is this old woman lying here,
My saint, who is a sacred shrine to your sister.
I have no desire for anything,
No Mecca other than my mother.
She has reached ninety-five years,
My old woman has fared badly.
When your mountain-like brother-in-law died,
Crying so much, "My foal,"
My mother was left in a dreadful state.
If we call her living, she is not among them.
This old woman here,
If we call her dead, she is not in the grave.
Though she can rise for the time it takes meat to cook,
She cannot stay up for many days.
She has no strength to stand upright.
Seen today, gone tomorrow,
When a mortal has grown old,
Such is this shit of a world!
Lie down, my revered mother,
Do not move, my mother!'
The great coat left by Manas
She brought over and spread upon her.
Your poor mother Chiyrdy
Made no audible cry,
Had no chance to let her voice out.
Biting the covering folded double,
She lay weeping in anguish,
Though she might die this very moment,
Imploring her only one, Semetey.
How could she refrain from weeping?
Her fate had not yet brought her death,
She had not yet seen the dark grave,
Had not yet braided her hair down her back.
Since her magnanimous Manas died,
Her lonely head had suffered torment,
Seen the night in the dark forest,
Made her living wandering in Bukhara.
To Temir Khan's city
She had come fleeing and wandering.
Cutting his twig,
Performing his rite,
Passing him over the dog's bowl,
Making him step over the sword's edge,
When he was six months old,
Still in his infant cradle,
She gave him to Ismail.
The aged old woman had not died.
Until her boy reached twelve,
She had not seen his fair face.
Now that the old woman lay down,
Let us leave her here
And begin with this side of the tale.
'My darling little brother,
Ride over and visit our home,
Keep eating food from my hand.
Come to the house without a master.
Come from time to time, little brother,
Keep seeing your sister's face.
My door is open; come and see,
Give me some of your attention.
"My sister is a widow," think,
And come learn how I fare.
I have been making a garment,
Brother dear as my life, wear it as you go!'
For many years in Bukhara,
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykei
Had she not lived?
'When my only child comes, he will wear it,' she thought.
A marten-fur cap an arm's length high,
Your dear mother Kanykei
Had she not been making?
Hiding it in a chest, weeping bitterly,
Setting it aside for her orphan Semetey,
Caring for it, stitching it firmly,
Entrusting it to her orphan,
Having gold worked into the tassels,
The marten and silver-fox skins
She had fashioned in the Kyrgyz manner.
From within the white chest,
Kanykei went around
And brought out an object.
If you look at each of its features,
A sorrowful tale, difficult words.
'Now, little brother, listen!
That your sister is a widow,
My companion-brother, come to know.
I shall give you a cap as a gift.
Let me take your suffering upon myself;
Do not be angry; wear it as you go!
Our land was in Talas,
Our people are the Kyrgyz blessed by Kyzyr.
All alike in deep crimson,
Such was its beauty.
Your fierce brother-in-law Manas—
Little brother, such was his cap.'
Then, saying these words,
She began from another side.
At that time Semetey,
What Semetey wore
Had otter fur one finger wide:
A round cap such as the Sarts wore.
She made him take off his cap,
Began to give him a different appearance,
Showing herself his elder sister,
